segments.he: פ"א על פורים באתה בת רבינו ז"ל מרת חי' ז"ל עם בנה נחמן ז"ל לברסלב והתאכסנה אצל א' מאנ"ש המובהקים ר' מרדכי ז"ל וספרו למהרנ"ת ז"ל שבת רבינו ז"ל עם בנה נחמן מתאכסנים בפורים אצל מרדכי והתפלא מוהרנ"ת ז"ל מהרמזים (שהי' מסתכל תמיד על הרמזים שבכל יום) ואמר השמעתם מה שספרו שנחמן מתאכסן בפורים אצל מרדכי "אז נחמן שטייט אן פורים בא מרדכי" וכן בשאר הזמנים (למשל ל"ג בעומר, אצל ר' שמעון וכו').
segments.en:
The Rav of Tcheryn gave Reb Baruch Ephraim two thousand gold coins for printing Parparaos LeChochmah, the new Likutay Eitzos, and the other smaller books. [The large books — Likutay Moharan and Likutay Tefilos — had a different story: a wealthy man in Breslov named Beril Leib Nekhilis was suddenly aroused to do a lasting rectification for his soul, knowing that the ultimate purpose is that "man is not accompanied by gold or silver." And when he recognized our fellowship as genuinely G-d-fearing, he decided to ask them what to do for his soul for eternity. He encountered one of our outstanding fellowship and spoke with him — and was told with great arousal. From then on he began to support our fellowship with regular weekly sustenance, and also gave money to print Likutay Moharan and so forth.] Reb Baruch Ephraim traveled with the money and printed the books. He returned with four hundred gold coins remaining. And the Rav of Tcheryn said: "Men darf aleyn shraybn un aleyn drukn un aleyn bazayn un aleyn lernen" — meaning: the Adversary places himself on the matters of Rabbainu so intensely that one must do everything oneself — write and print Rabbainu's books, as is known. He traveled without a passport. And the printing itself in Lemberg was done without permission — and he had enormous toil and exertion and self-sacrifice until the printing was complete. Afterward they searched for him with the books — and confiscated the books, giving them to the government bookbinder to use the pages for government book covers. But Reb Baruch Ephraim, through great effort and many pleas to the bookbinder — who was a religious Jew — after he found favor in his eyes, succeeded in arranging a scheme so that the bookbinder returned the books to him and used plain paper for the government covers. And Reb Baruch Ephraim himself was imprisoned in iron chains and remained imprisoned for some time — and could have spent all his days in prison. But Hashem helped: a fire broke out and everyone fled — and he fled too — until Hashem helped him and he returned home with the books.

And Reb Mendeli the Litvak, companion of Reb Baruch Ephraim, lived in Uman and his service was with great burning passion. People said of him that every day was with him: half a day of Yom Kippur and half a day of Simchas Torah — for until midday he prayed with such burning passion and arousal beyond all estimation, and afterward he would say to himself: "Mendeli — der Rebe hot dikh geheysin freylikh zayn — 'mitzvah gedolah lihyos besimchah tomid'!" [Mendeli — the Rebbe told you to be joyful — "It is a great mitzvah always to be in joy!"] Once the opponents slandered him before the governor, and the governor himself came to the kloiz to see him. He heard how he prayed and pleaded before Hashem with mercy, entreaty, and supplication — in a sweet, melodious voice. The governor was so moved that he shed tears and said: "If I were king I would give him whatever he wants." He was extremely poor — his entire livelihood was that at night he would make a few small cookies, and in the late afternoon after his prayer he would go to the marketplace to sell them. People would snatch them immediately, and other cookie bakers came close to him. And they said to him: "Reb Mendeli — what do you put into your cookies that people snatch them so?" He answered: "What can I tell you — they are kneaded in the weeping of midnight, and baked while in joy and song." For he kneaded them while reciting Tikkun Chatzos with tears — and baked them afterward in joy and song.
